items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: After I left McKinney’s, I had a job at the Empire Ballroom with my orchestra, and I managed to get Doc Cheatham to play with me in that orchestra.

ctx.x: After I left McKinney’s, I had a job at the Empire Ballroom with my orchestra, and I managed to get Doc Cheatham to play with me in that orchestra. He knew that I was interested in the trumpet, and so he encouraged me to, you know, play. I told him, well, I was afraid to play it. I was afraid it would impair my embouchure for the saxophone. He assured me that it wouldn’t, because he had also played saxophone. Of course, he didn’t say why he had given up the saxophone, you know. But he was such a wonderful trumpet…

ctx.x: All right. Let's go to the trumpet. Now when did you begin to go back to the trumpet? You had dropped it for the alto. When did you start returning to the trumpet?
Well, about 1929, I had an orchestra at the Arcadia Ballroom, I believe that was at 53rd Street and Broadway.

items.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995
items.q: performing with the big bands of Cab Calloway, Teddy Wilson, Benny Carter and Chick Webb

ctx.x: Doc Cheatham’s remarkable career in jazz reads like a fairy tale. Born Aldolphus Cheatham in 1905, he grew up in Nashville and took up the sax and trumpet at an early age. His first playing experience was at the Bijou Theater where he played behind Bessie Smith, later recording on the soprano sax with another blues great, Ma Rainey.
